topic: Minimal self-hosted execution path for scoped agent authority on BSC (chain 56) — EIP-7702 self-relay, no bundler, no vendor lock-in
executive_summary: A fully self-hosted path exists on BSC today and it is better than the bundler path. Verified live via BSC RPC (chain 0x38, Geth v1.7.7): the MetaMask Delegation Framework v1.3.0 is deployed on chain 56 — DelegationManager 0xdb9B1e94B5b69Df7e401DDbedE43491141047dB3 (11.5KB code), EIP7702StatelessDeleGatorImpl 0x63c0c19a282a1B52b07dD5a65b58948A07DAE32B (11.2KB), plus every caveat enforcer AiKi needs: ERC20PeriodTransferEnforcer, TimestampEnforcer, AllowedTargetsEnforcer, AllowedMethodsEnforcer, ValueLteEnforcer, LimitedCallsEnforcer, RedeemerEnforcer, MultiTokenPeriodEnforcer. Crucially ERC20PeriodTransferEnforcer is a RESETTING per-period cap ("the transferable amount resets at the beginning of each period"), which fixes the exact gap in Rhinestone's SmartSession on BSC, where ERC20SpendingLimitPolicy is lifetime-only and TimeFrame/UsageLimit/ValueLimit are not deployed at all. eth-infinitism's Simple7702Account is also live at 0xe6Cae83BdE06E4c305530e199D7217f42808555B (3.6KB) but enforces nothing — it is a batching shim, not scoped authority. Recommended path: AiKi self-relays a type-0x4 SetCode tx with viem 2.55.19 (`signAuthorization({account, contractAddress})` → `sendTransaction({authorizationList, to, data})`) to delegate the user EOA to EIP7702StatelessDeleGatorImpl, then AiKi's relayer calls `redeemDelegations` as the delegate and pays all gas in BNB. No bundler, no EntryPoint, no paymaster, no vendor API key. Estimated 5-8 eng days vs 8-14 for the 4337 route and 10-15 plus audit for a bespoke session-key contract. One honest caveat: DelegationManager carries a `whenNotPaused` modifier, so this is not zero third-party dependency — build a thin fallback executor behind an interface.

findings.claim: EIP-7702 self-relay works on BSC with a plain RPC and no bundler; viem 2.55.19 exposes signAuthorization + sendTransaction({authorizationList})
findings.detail: Verified npm registry: viem latest is 2.55.19 (fetched 2026-08-19), confirming the 2.55.x line. viem docs give the exact shape: `walletClient.signAuthorization({ account: eoa, contractAddress })` returns an Authorization with fields `chainId`, `contractAddress`, `nonce`, `r`, `s`, `yParity`. The field is `contractAddress`, NOT `address`. Optional params: `chainId` (defaults to client chain), `nonce` (defaults to the account's next nonce), and `executor: 'self' | undefined`. Set `executor: 'self'` ONLY when the same account that signed the authorization also sends the transaction (this changes the nonce accounting). For AiKi's sponsored model the relayer is a different account, so `executor` is omitted. The transaction is then a normal `eth_sendRawTransaction` of a type-0x4 envelope: `sendTransaction({ authorizationList: [authorization], to: eoa.address, data })`. There is no bundler, no EntryPoint, and no ERC-4337 UserOperation anywhere in this path. BSC accepts type 0x4 since Pascal (2025-03-20, previously verified).

findings.claim: Two 7702 delegation targets are confirmed live on BSC by direct eth_getCode — but only one enforces anything
findings.detail: Queried https://bsc-dataseed.bnbchain.org (eth_chainId = 0x38, clientVersion Geth/v1.7.7) on 2026-08-19. Simple7702Account (eth-infinitism, the EntryPoint v0.8 'delegatee' address per Candide docs): 0xe6Cae83BdE06E4c305530e199D7217f42808555B returns 7316 hex chars (~3.6KB bytecode) — DEPLOYED. MetaMask EIP7702StatelessDeleGatorImpl: 0x63c0c19a282a1B52b07dD5a65b58948A07DAE32B returns 22408 bytes (~11.2KB) — DEPLOYED. EntryPoint v0.8 0x4337084D9E255Ff0702461CF8895CE9E3b5Ff108 returns 43514 bytes, re-confirming prior research. The critical distinction: Simple7702Account gives batching and 4337 compatibility but has NO scoping primitive — an EOA delegated to it grants all-or-nothing authority to itself, so AiKi would have to hold the user's key or enforce limits purely off-chain. EIP7702StatelessDeleGatorImpl stores no signer state (control is granted to the EOA sharing the same address) and is the entry point into the caveat-enforced delegation system. For scoped agent authority, Simple7702Account is the wrong target. Kernel/Safe7702 addresses were not resolved and remain unverified.

findings.claim: MetaMask Delegation Framework v1.3.0 (ERC-7710) is deployed on BSC mainnet — contracts confirmed by bytecode, not just documentation
findings.detail: The framework's Deployments.md lists 'Binance Smart Chain' in its mainnet set and states deployments use a CREATE2 salt of 'GATOR' so addresses are identical across chains. I verified this against chain 56 rather than trusting the doc. eth_getCode on 2026-08-19 returned non-empty bytecode for: DelegationManager 0xdb9B1e94B5b69Df7e401DDbedE43491141047dB3 (23044 bytes), SimpleFactory 0x69Aa2f9fe1572F1B640E1bbc512f5c3a734fc77c (1540), ERC20PeriodTransferEnforcer 0x474e3Ae7E169e940607cC624Da8A15Eb120139aB (6730), TimestampEnforcer 0x1046bb45C8d673d4ea75321280DB34899413c069 (2548), AllowedTargetsEnforcer 0x7F20f61b1f09b08D970938F6fa563634d65c4EeB (3730), AllowedMethodsEnforcer 0x2c21fD0Cb9DC8445CB3fb0DC5E7Bb0Aca01842B5 (4126), ValueLteEnforcer 0x92Bf12322527cAA612fd31a0e810472BBB106A8F (2582), LimitedCallsEnforcer 0x04658B29F6b82ed55274221a06Fc97D318E25416 (2552), RedeemerEnforcer 0xE144b0b2618071B4E56f746313528a669c7E65c5 (3260), ERC20StreamingEnforcer 0x56c97aE02f233B29fa03502Ecc0457266d9be00e (5920), MultiTokenPeriodEnforcer 0xFB2f1a9BD76d3701B730E5d69C3219D42D80eBb7 (10556), NativeTokenPeriodTransferEnforcer 0x9BC0FAf4Aca5AE429F4c06aEEaC517520CB16BD9 (5844). Byte counts are JSON response sizes, all far above an empty '0x' result.

findings.claim: ERC20PeriodTransferEnforcer is a RESETTING periodic cap — this is the single most important finding, because it closes the gap Rhinestone leaves open on BSC
findings.detail: Read from source. Natspec: 'The transferable amount resets at the beginning of each period, and any unused tokens are forfeited once the period ends.' Confirmed in `_getAvailableAmount`: `uint256 alreadyTransferred = isNewPeriod_ ? 0 : _allowance.transferredInCurrentPeriod;`. Terms are a packed 116-byte blob: token address (bytes 0-19), periodAmount uint256 (20-51), periodDuration in seconds (52-83), startDate timestamp (84-115). It requires the call's calldata selector to equal `IERC20.transfer.selector` (0xa9059cbb) and emits `TransferredInPeriod`. Errors include 'transfer-amount-exceeded', 'transfer-not-started', 'invalid-zero-period-amount', 'invalid-zero-period-duration', 'invalid-zero-start-date'. Contrast with prior verified research: Rhinestone's ERC20SpendingLimitPolicy on BSC is a LIFETIME cap with monotonic alreadySpent and no block.timestamp, and the TimeFrame/UsageLimit/ValueLimit policies are NOT deployed on 56. So 'agent may spend 50 BUSD per day' is expressible on BSC via the MetaMask framework and is NOT expressible via Rhinestone SmartSession on BSC. Note the selector restriction: this enforcer covers transfer only, not approve or transferFrom.

findings.claim: What the chain enforces in the ERC-7710 path: signature, authority chain, delegate identity, revocation, and every caveat hook
findings.detail: From DelegationManager.sol source. Entry point is `redeemDelegations(bytes[] _permissionContexts, ModeCode[] _modes, bytes[] _executionCallDatas) external whenNotPaused`. On-chain validation, all unavoidable by AiKi: (1) delegator signature — ECDSA.recover must equal delegation.delegator, else InvalidEOASignature; for contract delegators IERC1271.isValidSignature must return the magic value; (2) authority chain linkage — each delegation's `authority` must equal the next delegation hash, and the terminal one must equal ROOT_AUTHORITY; (3) delegate chain — successive delegates must match delegators unless ANY_DELEGATE; (4) caller identity — `if (delegations_[0].delegate != msg.sender && delegations_[0].delegate != ANY_DELEGATE) revert InvalidDelegate()`; (5) revocation — `if (disabledDelegations[hash]) revert CannotUseADisabledDelegation()`; (6) caveat hooks — beforeAllHook and beforeHook on every enforcer before execution, afterHook and afterAllHook in reverse order after. Structs: Delegation{delegator, delegate, authority, caveats[], salt, signature}, Caveat{enforcer, terms, args}. Everything else — which agent may act, task semantics, marketplace policy, UX — is enforced by AiKi off-chain and is not a chain guarantee.

findings.claim: Gas sponsorship is trivially solved by self-relay: AiKi's relayer is the tx sender and pays BNB; the user never holds BNB and never signs a transaction
findings.detail: There are two separate sponsored moments. (a) Delegation install: the user signs only an EIP-7702 authorization tuple off-chain (chainId, contractAddress, nonce, r, s, yParity). AiKi wraps it in `authorizationList` of a transaction AiKi sends and pays for. Because the executor is AiKi and not the signer, do NOT pass `executor: 'self'`. (b) Action execution: AiKi's relayer EOA is the `delegate` and calls DelegationManager.redeemDelegations directly, satisfying the `delegations_[0].delegate == msg.sender` check, and pays gas. No paymaster, no EntryPoint, no bundler, no deposit staking. Trust implications, stated honestly: AiKi gains liveness power (ordering, timing, censorship, refusal to relay) but NOT custody — it cannot exceed the caveats, because the enforcers revert. Real risks to design around: 7702 authorization signed with chainId 0 is replayable on every chain, so always pin chainId 56; the authorization nonce is the user EOA's account nonce, so any user-initiated transaction in between invalidates a pre-signed authorization and requires re-signing; a compromised relayer key can act freely within caveat bounds, so scope one delegate key per agent and keep periods tight.

findings.claim: Honest three-way comparison for a 3-week deadline: 7702 self-relay + delegation framework wins on both risk and eng days
findings.detail: Option A, bundler ERC-4337: EntryPoint v0.6/v0.7/v0.8 are live on 56, but this route reintroduces the exact vendor dependency being avoided (bundler RPC, paymaster service, API keys, rate limits), and on BSC the Rhinestone policy set cannot express a resetting daily cap. Est. 8-14 eng days including vendor evaluation, UserOperation plumbing, paymaster integration, module install flows, plus unquantified vendor-availability risk. Option B, 7702 self-relay + MetaMask Delegation Framework: plain RPC, contracts already deployed and verified on 56, richest on-chain policy set available on this chain. Est. 5-8 eng days: 1-2 for the 7702 authorization and relay path, 2-3 for delegation construction/caveat encoding/signing UX, 1 for the relayer service and nonce management, 1-2 for testnet-to-mainnet hardening. Option C, bespoke AiKi session-key contract: maximum control and zero third-party pause risk, but 10-15 eng days plus a 2-4 week audit that does not fit before 9 Sep 2026. Shipping it unaudited while it holds delegated spend authority is the worst risk on the table. Recommendation: B now, C later behind an interface.

findings.claim: The one genuine dependency in Option B: DelegationManager is pausable, so 'no vendor dependency' is not literally true
findings.detail: redeemDelegations carries the `whenNotPaused` modifier. If the DelegationManager owner on BSC pauses the contract, every AiKi delegation redemption halts until unpaused. This is a liveness dependency on a third party — weaker than a bundler dependency (no API key, no rate limit, no per-request business relationship, and the code is immutable and CREATE2-deterministic) but it is not zero. Funds are never at risk from a pause; only the ability to execute is. Two mitigations worth the eng time: (1) put redemption behind an `IAgentExecutor` interface in AiKi's relayer so a fallback path can be swapped in without touching call sites; (2) build the minimal bespoke session-key executor from Option C as a post-deadline fallback, since it becomes cheap once the delegation-encoding and relayer layers already exist. I did not verify the pause owner's identity or whether it is a multisig/timelock on chain 56 — that check should happen before mainnet launch, since it determines how real this risk is.

interfaces.name: AiKi self-relay: install 7702 delegation, sponsored (viem 2.55.19)
DelegationManager.redeemDelegations — the chain-enforced execution entry point
ERC20PeriodTransferEnforcer terms encoding — resetting daily cap (116 bytes packed)
Recommended AiKi caveat stack — all addresses bytecode-verified on chain 56
interfaces.source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MetaMask/delegation-framework/main/documents/Deployments.md, each address confirmed non-empty by eth_getCode on chain 56

gaps: Did NOT verify that the @metamask/delegation-toolkit npm package supports chain 56 in its own chain config. The CONTRACTS are on BSC (bytecode-confirmed), but the SDK may not ship a 56 entry — budget half a day to override addresses manually, and treat the SDK as optional since redeemDelegations can be called with a raw viem ABI.

ERC-7715 (wallet_grantPermissions) support in the MetaMask wallet client for BSC is entirely unverified. ERC-7710 on-chain redemption is confirmed; the wallet-side permission-request UX is not. Do not assume users can grant via MetaMask UI on BSC — AiKi likely needs its own signing flow for the Delegation struct (EIP-712).

Never sent a live type-0x4 transaction. eth_getCode reads confirm deployment; they do not prove that public BSC RPC providers accept eth_sendRawTransaction for type 0x4 envelopes. Send one throwaway 7702 tx on BSC testnet then mainnet in week 1 — this is the single highest-value de-risking action and costs under an hour.

DelegationManager's pause authority on chain 56 was not inspected — owner address, whether it is an EOA/multisig/timelock. This determines whether the whenNotPaused dependency is a footnote or a real risk. Check owner() before mainnet.

Enforcer bytecode was confirmed present but NOT diffed against the audited source, and BscScan source-verification status was not checked. CREATE2 determinism makes a mismatch unlikely but it is unproven.

Kernel (ZeroDev) and Safe7702 implementation addresses on BSC were not resolved — the searches did not surface published 56 addresses. If MetaMask's framework is rejected, these are unmapped alternatives.

EntryPoint v0.9 and Simple7702AccountV09 now exist (Candide docs call V09 'recommended for new integrations'), but neither was verified on chain 56. Irrelevant to the recommended path, which touches no EntryPoint at all.
Gas cost of a type-0x4 SetCode tx and of redeemDelegations on BSC was not measured. Needed to price AiKi's sponsorship burn per user and per agent action.
aiki_implications: Take the 7702 self-relay path and drop the bundler question entirely. The recommended stack is: viem 2.55.19 + a type-0x4 SetCode tx delegating the user EOA to EIP7702StatelessDeleGatorImpl 0x63c0c19a282a1B52b07dD5a65b58948A07DAE32B, then AiKi's relayer calling DelegationManager 0xdb9B1e94B5b69Df7e401DDbedE43491141047dB3. No bundler, no EntryPoint, no paymaster, no API key, no vendor rate limit. Est. 5-8 eng days, which fits the 9 Sep 2026 deadline with margin.

This reverses the earlier Rhinestone-leaning conclusion and should be escalated. Rhinestone SmartSession on BSC cannot express 'agent may spend 50 BUSD per day' — its ERC20SpendingLimitPolicy is a lifetime cap, and TimeFrame/UsageLimit/ValueLimit are not deployed on 56. The MetaMask framework's ERC20PeriodTransferEnforcer resets every period, and TimestampEnforcer/LimitedCallsEnforcer/ValueLteEnforcer are all confirmed live on 56. For a marketplace whose core promise is a recurring bounded budget per agent, this is the difference between shipping the real product and shipping a degraded one.

Be precise in all user-facing and investor-facing copy about the chain/AiKi enforcement split. CHAIN-ENFORCED: per-period spend ceiling, delegation expiry, target-contract allowlist, method-selector allowlist, native-value ceiling, call count, which agent key may redeem, delegator signature validity, revocation via disabledDelegations. AIKI-ENFORCED (trust us, off-chain): agent selection and reputation, task semantics, pricing, matching, whether a spend was 'appropriate', and relay liveness/ordering. Never let marketing blur the second list into the first.

Design the delegation as one delegation per agent per user, with a distinct delegate key per agent. RedeemerEnforcer pins redemption to a specific key, so a compromise of one agent's relayer key cannot touch another agent's authority. Combine with a short TimestampEnforcer window so stale delegations expire without requiring an on-chain revoke.

Block approve() explicitly. ERC20PeriodTransferEnforcer only constrains calldata whose selector is IERC20.transfer (0xa9059cbb) — it says nothing about approve or transferFrom. Without AllowedMethodsEnforcer (0x2c21fD0Cb9DC8445CB3fb0DC5E7Bb0Aca01842B5) restricting selectors, an agent could grant an unlimited allowance to a third party and drain around the period cap. This is the most likely way to ship a fake safety guarantee.

Handle the 7702 nonce coupling in the relayer from day one. The authorization's nonce is the user EOA's account nonce, so any user-initiated transaction between signing and relaying silently invalidates it. Detect this, re-request the signature, and never leave a user staring at an unexplained failure — this will otherwise be the top support issue at launch.

Pin chainId 56 in every signAuthorization call. chainId 0 authorizations are valid on every EVM chain; signing one would let the same user signature install a delegation on chains AiKi never intended. Make this a lint rule, not a convention.

Budget one day in week 1 to send a real type-0x4 transaction on BSC testnet and mainnet. Everything in this research is read-only verification; the entire plan rests on public BSC RPCs accepting type-0x4 envelopes, which is assumed from Pascal but untested here.

Put redemption behind an IAgentExecutor interface. DelegationManager's whenNotPaused modifier is a genuine third-party liveness dependency — smaller than a bundler dependency, but real. The abstraction costs about half a day now and makes the bespoke session-key executor a drop-in later, converting Option C from a rewrite into a post-deadline upgrade.

Note that AiKi's sponsorship model becomes very clean: users need zero BNB and never sign a transaction, only an off-chain authorization and an EIP-712 delegation. That is a materially better onboarding story than the 4337 route and worth featuring — but price it first, since AiKi pays gas for both the delegation install and every agent action.

topic: ERC-4337 bundler and paymaster availability on BNB Smart Chain (chain 56), and whether EIP-7702 + EntryPoint v0.8 removes the third-party bundler dependency for AiKi
executive_summary: This is NOT a blocker. Chain 56 is served by a live, production ERC-4337 bundler today, verified by direct RPC calls (not docs). Pimlico's public bundler at https://public.pimlico.io/v2/56/rpc answered eth_chainId with "0x38" and eth_supportedEntryPoints with FOUR EntryPoints, all of which I confirmed hold bytecode on chain 56. Its gas oracle (pimlico_getUserOperationGasPrice) also answers live on 56, returning ~3 gwei — proof of a real, priced, operating service rather than a stub route. Biconomy documents full BSC mainnet support (bundler + sponsorship paymaster + token paymaster, EP v0.7, Nexus v1.0.2, MEE up to 2.2.2). Etherspot/Skandha and thirdweb both route chain 56 (they reject on missing credentials, never on unsupported chain). Candide/Voltaire showed no chain-56 route. Alchemy Gas Manager on 56 is unconfirmed; Stackup's hosted endpoint did not respond. Separately, BNB Chain operates its OWN native sponsorship rail — BSC Paymaster / NodeReal MegaFuel — but it sponsors plain EOA transactions via BEP-322 PBS, not 4337 userOps. On the secondary question: EntryPoint.handleOps is permissionless, so AiKi can self-relay userOps from its own EOA with no third-party bundler at all. That is the correct architecture here, because Rhinestone SmartSession is an ERC-7579 *validator* (validateUserOp) and therefore requires the EntryPoint path — it cannot be driven by a bare 7702 direct call. Answer: yes, AiKi can execute session-key transactions on BSC mainnet today.

findings.claim: Pimlico's bundler is LIVE on chain 56 and serves four EntryPoints — verified by direct RPC, not documentation.
findings.detail: POST to https://public.pimlico.io/v2/56/rpc with eth_supportedEntryPoints returned: ["0x5FF137D4b0FDCD49DcA30c7CF57E578a026d2789","0x0000000071727De22E5E9d8BAf0edAc6f37da032","0x4337084D9E255Ff0702461CF8895CE9E3b5Ff108","0x433709009B8330FDa32311DF1C2AFA402eD8D009"]. eth_chainId on the same endpoint returned "0x38" (=56). Note the chain must be given NUMERICALLY: https://public.pimlico.io/v2/bsc/rpc returns error -32000 'chain "bsc" is not supported'. Testnet works too — /v2/97/rpc returned the identical four-EntryPoint list, so BSC testnet is available for staging. Documented public-endpoint shape is https://public.pimlico.io/v2/{chain_id}/rpc at 20 requests/minute/IP, which is fine for development but not production.

findings.claim: Pimlico's authenticated endpoint shape for BSC is https://api.pimlico.io/v2/56/rpc?apikey=YOUR_KEY — confirmed by the server's own error.
findings.detail: POST to https://api.pimlico.io/v2/56/rpc without a key returned {"statusCode":401,"error":"Unauthorized","message":"missing 'apikey' query parameter"}. The 401-on-auth (rather than an unsupported-chain error like the 'bsc' slug produced) proves chain 56 is a valid route on the paid API and that the key is passed as a query parameter, not a header. Pimlico serves bundler and paymaster on a single API surface, so the same base URL is used for pm_* paymaster methods with the sponsorship policy configured in their dashboard.

findings.claim: Pimlico's gas oracle answers on 56, proving a real priced service rather than a routing stub.
findings.detail: pimlico_getUserOperationGasPrice on https://public.pimlico.io/v2/56/rpc returned {"slow":{"maxFeePerGas":"0x3938700","maxPriorityFeePerGas":"0x3938700"},"standard":{"maxFeePerGas":"0x3c14dc0",...},"fast":{"maxFeePerGas":"0x3ef1480",...}}. That is 0.06 / 0.063 / 0.066 gwei tiers. BSC gas is cheap enough that sponsoring AiKi's session-key transactions is close to free in absolute terms — a 200k-gas userOp costs on the order of 1.3e-5 BNB. Note maxFee == maxPriorityFee on all three tiers, which is the expected shape for BSC's fee market.

findings.claim: A FOURTH EntryPoint exists on chain 56 beyond the three prior research verified — 0x433709009B8330FDa32311DF1C2AFA402eD8D009 — and Pimlico serves it.
findings.detail: eth_getCode against BSC mainnet returned code lengths of: v0.6 0x5FF137D4... = 23689 bytes; v0.7 0x00000000717... = 16035 bytes; v0.8 0x4337084D... = 21738 bytes; and 0x433709009B8330FDa32311DF1C2AFA402eD8D009 = 22425 bytes. All four are deployed and non-empty. The fourth is almost certainly a patched v0.8.x point release (its bytecode is close in size to v0.8 but distinct). AiKi should determine which of 0x4337084D... and 0x433709... is the canonical v0.8 target before committing, since account factories and SmartSession registrations are EntryPoint-scoped and migrating later is painful.

findings.claim: Biconomy documents full BSC mainnet support including a sponsorship paymaster and a token paymaster.
findings.detail: Biconomy's supported-chains page lists 'BSC Mainnet' under the MEE stack with versions 2.2.2, 2.2.1, 2.1.0, 2.0.0, 1.1.0, 1.0.0, offering bundler, sponsorship, token paymaster and smart-account execution. Under the legacy ERC-4337 section, 'Binance Smart Chain Mainnet' and 'Binance Smart Chain Testnet' both show full support for EntryPoint v0.7.0 with bundler, sponsorship paymaster, token paymaster, contracts and Nexus v1.0.2 all enabled. Access is via a dashboard API key on the Supertransaction tab. Caveat: this is EntryPoint v0.7 only — Biconomy is NOT a v0.8/7702 path, and Nexus is its own account, so pairing it with Rhinestone SmartSession needs verification.

findings.claim: Etherspot/Skandha routes chain 56 and Skandha supports EntryPoint v0.8 — and it is open source and self-hostable.
findings.detail: POST to https://rpc.etherspot.io/v2/56 returned {"message":"Api key not found, visit https://etherspot.fyi for more information"} — an authentication rejection, not an unsupported-chain rejection, which means 56 is a live route. Etherspot has publicly announced Skandha bundler support for EntryPoint v0.8.0. The strategic value here is less the hosted service and more that Skandha (like Pimlico's Alto and Alchemy's Rundler, Apache-2.0) is open-source: AiKi can run its own bundler on 56 rather than depending on any vendor's chain-56 roadmap.

findings.claim: thirdweb routes chain 56 on its bundler; ZeroDev's URL shape is known but chain-56 support is unverified.
findings.detail: POST to https://56.bundler.thirdweb.com/v2 returned {"error":"The client id is missing. Make sure it is included with your x-client-id request header.","code":"MISSING_CLIENT_ID"} — again an auth rejection, so chain 56 is routed; the chain id goes in the SUBDOMAIN and the key in an x-client-id header. The slug form https://bsc.bundler.thirdweb.com returned {"error":"Invalid chain: bsc"}, so numeric only. ZeroDev's documented shape is https://rpc.zerodev.app/api/v3/[PROJECT_ID]/chain/[CHAIN_ID]?provider=[ULTRA_RELAY|ALCHEMY|GELATO|PIMLICO] — it multiplexes over other bundlers, so its BSC coverage likely inherits from Pimlico. ZeroDev Kernel v3.3 on BNB is reported in secondary sources but I could not verify chain 56 from ZeroDev's own docs.

findings.claim: Candide/Voltaire shows NO chain-56 route; Stackup's endpoint did not respond; Alchemy Gas Manager on 56 is unconfirmed.
findings.detail: https://api.candide.dev/bundler/v3/bsc returned {"message":"Route POST:/bundler/v3/bsc not found","statusCode":404} and numeric variants produced no route either. Candide's own docs page would not render for fetch. https://api.stackup.sh/v1/node/56 returned empty — consistent with Stackup having wound down its hosted bundler, though I did not confirm that. For Alchemy, search of their Gas Manager and Rundler documentation surfaced coverage described as Ethereum, Base, Arbitrum, Optimism and Polygon with BNB Chain NOT called out for Gas Manager; Alchemy does sell a plain BNB RPC, which is a different product. Treat all three as unavailable for AiKi's purposes absent further evidence.

findings.claim: BNB Chain operates its own native gas-sponsorship rail (BSC Paymaster / NodeReal MegaFuel) but it is for plain EOA transactions, NOT ERC-4337 userOps.
findings.detail: BNB Chain documents a 'paymaster solution specifically designed for Externally Owned Account (EOA) wallets', which lets wallets set gas price to zero on potentially-sponsored transactions; sponsorship is settled through the BEP-322 Proposer-Builder Separation architecture, with builders incorporating sponsored bundles into blocks. NodeReal's MegaFuel is the reference implementation and lets sponsors customise policy; Bitget Wallet has integrated it. Critically this is a SEPARATE rail from ERC-4337 — it sponsors ordinary transactions, so it composes with a plain EIP-7702 direct-call design but does not sponsor userOps. The docs do not state pricing, limits, or whether type-4 (7702) transactions are eligible. I found no evidence that BNB Chain, NodeReal, or BlockRazor operates an ERC-4337 bundler.

findings.claim: EntryPoint.handleOps is permissionless, so AiKi can self-relay userOps with no third-party bundler — this is the real answer to the blocker.
findings.detail: The 'bundler' in ERC-4337 is not a privileged role. handleOps(ops, beneficiary) can be called by any address; the bundler's only job is to simulate, batch, and submit, and it is repaid from the account's EntryPoint deposit or the paymaster's deposit to the beneficiary address it names. AiKi can therefore run a backend EOA that calls handleOps directly against the v0.8 EntryPoint on 56 — no Pimlico, no API key, no rate limit, no vendor chain-support roadmap risk. For sponsorship, AiKi deploys its OWN paymaster contract, stakes and deposits it in the EntryPoint, and signs paymasterAndData off-chain from its backend. The costs of self-relaying are real but bounded: you lose vendor-run mempool/replacement logic, gas estimation (you must run simulateHandleOp yourself), and nonce/throughput management on the relayer EOA under concurrency.

findings.claim: EntryPoint v0.8 has native EIP-7702 support, including a bundled Simple7702Account and a 0x7702 initCode marker.
findings.detail: The v0.8.0 release adds Simple7702Account to the core distribution — described as a fully audited minimalist smart contract wallet that can be safely authorized by any EOA, with support for the major smart-account features. initCode carrying the 0x7702 prefix marks a 7702 delegation rather than a factory deployment, and an EIP7702AccountInitialized event exposes the delegation target. v0.8 also moved to ERC-712-based userOp hashing and signatures, which changes the signing surface versus v0.7 — AiKi's session-key signer must implement the v0.8 domain, not reuse v0.7 hashing. Combined with prior research confirming 7702 has been live on BSC since Pascal (2025-03-20) with ~1.4% of txs type 0x4, the v0.8 + 7702 path is available on chain 56.

findings.claim: Rhinestone SmartSession CANNOT be driven by a bare 7702 direct call — it is an ERC-7579 validator and requires the EntryPoint path.
findings.detail: Reading the local ISmartSession.sol interface confirms SmartSession exposes validateUserOp (documented as the 'ERC4337/ERC7579 validation function' that dissects userOp.signature to parse out a PermissionId), plus onInstall/onUninstall/isModuleType and isValidSignatureWithSender for ERC-1271. There is no direct 'execute with session key' entry point. This is the decisive architectural constraint: if AiKi wants Rhinestone SmartSession policies (SpendingLimits/UniversalAction/Sudo, which prior research confirmed are deployed on 56), transactions MUST be packaged as userOps and routed through an EntryPoint. You cannot skip 4337 and have a relayer call the 7702-delegated EOA directly while still getting SmartSession enforcement. You CAN skip the third-party bundler, because handleOps is permissionless.

gaps: Which of 0x4337084D9E255Ff0702461CF8895CE9E3b5Ff108 and 0x433709009B8330FDa32311DF1C2AFA402eD8D009 is the CANONICAL v0.8 EntryPoint to build against on 56. Both hold bytecode (21738 vs 22425 bytes) and Pimlico serves both. This must be resolved before registering SmartSession permissions, since they are EntryPoint-scoped. Verify by comparing deployed bytecode against eth-infinitism v0.8.0 vs v0.8.x release artifacts.

I did NOT verify a Pimlico PAYMASTER (pm_getPaymasterStubData / pm_sponsorUserOperation) actually sponsors on 56 — the public endpoint requires a key for paymaster methods, so gas sponsorship on 56 via Pimlico is inferred from their ERC-20 paymaster marketing, not proven. Get a free API key and call pm_getPaymasterStubData against chain 56 before committing to sponsored UX.

No pricing or free-tier numbers were obtained for ANY provider on chain 56. Pimlico, Biconomy, Etherspot and thirdweb all gate pricing behind dashboards. Budget impact of sponsorship at AiKi's expected transaction volume is unquantified.

Whether Rhinestone SmartSession works with an EIP-7702-delegated EOA on 56 specifically, versus a conventionally-deployed ERC-7579 account. SmartSession's onInstall must run against the delegated account; the 7702 + module-install bootstrap flow on 56 is untested here.

Whether BSC Paymaster / MegaFuel accepts type-4 (EIP-7702) transactions for sponsorship. The BNB Chain docs discuss BEP-322 bundles and zero gas price but say nothing about transaction type 0x4. This matters if AiKi wants the native sponsorship rail instead of a 4337 paymaster.
Stackup's status is genuinely unknown — the endpoint returned nothing, which is consistent with either a wrong URL or a shut-down service. Do not report Stackup as dead without a second check.

ZeroDev chain-56 support was not confirmed from ZeroDev's own documentation, only from secondary sources. Since ZeroDev multiplexes over Pimlico/Alchemy/Gelato, its BSC coverage probably inherits from Pimlico, but the Kernel v3.3 deployment addresses on 56 were not verified.
Alchemy Gas Manager on 56: absence of evidence, not evidence of absence. The search did not surface a definitive supported-networks table.
aiki_implications: ANSWER: YES — AiKi can execute session-key transactions on BSC mainnet today. The stack is: Rhinestone SmartSession (validator, deployed on 56) on an ERC-7579 account, userOps routed to an EntryPoint on 56, submitted either via Pimlico (verified live) or via AiKi's own relayer calling handleOps. The bundler question is not a blocker and should be closed.

RECOMMENDED ARCHITECTURE: self-relay as the primary path, Pimlico as the fallback. Because handleOps is permissionless, AiKi's backend EOA can submit userOps directly — this removes vendor rate limits (Pimlico's public tier is only 20 req/min/IP), removes API-key dependency, removes any risk that a vendor deprioritises chain 56, and gives full control over inclusion. Wire Pimlico's authenticated endpoint as a hot fallback so a relayer outage or nonce-stall does not halt the marketplace.

DO NOT design around 'EIP-7702 lets us skip 4337 entirely'. That is the tempting conclusion and it is wrong for AiKi specifically. SmartSession exposes only validateUserOp — a 7579 validator hook — so a relayer calling the 7702-delegated EOA directly gets NO SmartSession policy enforcement. Dropping EntryPoint means dropping SmartSession, which means rebuilding session-key policy from scratch and discarding the Rhinestone audit surface. Keep EntryPoint; drop only the third-party bundler.

7702's actual value to AiKi is onboarding, not execution: users keep their existing EOA address and delegate to a 7579 implementation rather than deploying a counterfactual smart account and migrating funds. That is a meaningful UX win for an agent marketplace where users arrive with funded BSC EOAs. Budget engineering time for the 7702 delegation + module-bootstrap flow, and validate it on BSC testnet (Pimlico's /v2/97/rpc works) before mainnet.

EntryPoint version decision is now urgent and is on the critical path to 9 Sep. v0.8 changed userOp hashing to ERC-712 domains, so the session-key signer implementation differs between v0.7 and v0.8 and is not portable. v0.8 is required if you want native 7702 support. But resolve the 0x4337084D vs 0x433709 ambiguity FIRST — registering SmartSession permissions against the wrong EntryPoint is expensive to unwind.

Gas sponsorship has two independent rails on BSC and AiKi should pick deliberately. Rail A: a 4337 paymaster (Pimlico's, Biconomy's, or AiKi's own staked contract) sponsoring userOps. Rail B: BNB Chain's native BSC Paymaster / NodeReal MegaFuel, which sponsors plain EOA transactions via BEP-322 and does NOT understand userOps. Since AiKi is committed to the EntryPoint path for SmartSession, Rail A is the correct choice — and deploying AiKi's own paymaster keeps the zero-third-party-dependency property end to end.

Sponsorship cost is a non-issue at BSC gas prices. Pimlico's live oracle on 56 returned ~0.06 gwei standard; a 200k-gas userOp is on the order of 1.3e-5 BNB. AiKi can sponsor aggressively for user acquisition without material treasury impact. The real cost of sponsorship is abuse control (rate limits, per-user caps), not gas.

Combine with the known ERC20SpendingLimitPolicy limitation. Prior research established that policy is a LIFETIME cap with monotonic alreadySpent and no time component, and that TimeFrame/UsageLimit/ValueLimit policies are NOT deployed on 56. Since AiKi is self-relaying anyway, enforce per-period and per-usage limits in the RELAYER before signing/submitting, and treat the on-chain lifetime cap as the backstop. Self-relaying makes this straightforward — you already control the submission gate.

Biconomy is the strongest documented fallback if the Rhinestone/SmartSession path stalls: full BSC mainnet support with bundler, sponsorship paymaster and token paymaster on EntryPoint v0.7 with Nexus v1.0.2. But it is a v0.7-only, Nexus-account path — adopting it means giving up 7702-native onboarding and re-verifying SmartSession compatibility with Nexus. Treat it as a plan-C pivot, not a parallel track.

Concrete next actions, in order: (1) resolve which v0.8 EntryPoint is canonical on 56; (2) get a free Pimlico key and prove pm_getPaymasterStubData sponsors on chain 56; (3) prototype the self-relay loop — simulateHandleOp via eth_call, then handleOps from a backend EOA — on BSC testnet via /v2/97/rpc; (4) test SmartSession onInstall against a 7702-delegated EOA on 56. Items 1 and 3 are the schedule risk.
